data.title: France's Catholic influencers take faith from social media to real life
data.description: Catholic influencers gathered hundreds of young people for an evening of prayer at Paris's Saint-Sulpice church ahead of Pope Leo XIV's visit, highlighting how social media is becoming a new tool for evangelisation. data.title: Pope Leo XIV's Paris agenda includes Macron meeting and Notre-Dame visit
data.description: Paris is making final preparations for Pope Leo XIV's first official visit to the French capital in 18 years, with volunteers welcoming crowds ahead of his four-day trip. His programme includes meetings with President Emmanuel Macron and UNESCO, a popemobile procession, a prayer service at Notre-Dame, a youth vigil at the Stade de France, and a mass at Place de la Concorde expected to draw up to one million people before he continues to Lourdes and Metz.

data.title: Pope Leo XIV's France visit puts Macron in diplomatic balancing act
data.description: Pope Leo XIV's visit to France is forcing Emmanuel Macron into a delicate diplomatic balancing act. As both the head of the Catholic Church and the head of the Vatican City State, the pontiff requires the French president to navigate the country's secular traditions carefully. There will be no private meeting between the two leaders — officially because of the Pope's packed schedule — and Macron is not expected to attend any of the religious services during the visit. FRANCE 24's Rochelle Ferguson has the details.

data.title: ‘Most powerful force is human potential’: Ukraine's military prioritises new tactics, technologies
data.description: François Picard is pleased to welcome Kyrylo Berkal, Deputy Commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, He sees Ukraine’s struggle centred on human potential, adaptation and will. While Ukraine is outnumbered, outgunned and sometimes outflanked, their answer is to make human initiative a weapon: giving soldiers and sergeants room to innovate, developing technology from the tactical level upward, and trying to outthink their adversary. Berkal says that Operation Vivaldi embodies that philosophy.

data.title: 'Send in the Clowns': Viral video fuels claims Denmark trolled Trump and Rubio
data.description: A viral video claims Danish officials played Judy Collins’ “Send in the Clowns” as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived for a Greenland signing ceremony, sparking claims of Danish “trolling”. Our checks of separate livestreams confirm the song really played and the video was not manipulated. Denmark has denied choosing the music, while the UN says it did not organise the event. Whilst the song was real, there is no evidence Denmark selected it deliberately. Vedika Bahl fact-checks.

data.title: The future of AI in their hands? Trump-Xi summit dismisses calls for global oversight
data.description: It's their AI world and we're just living in it. If that's the feeling of those who suffer from AI anxiety, it may worsen watching the Chinese president's first state visit to Washington in nine years. If there's one issue that the planet's biggest superpowers agree on, it's that now is not the time for global regulation of artificial intelligence. As they sit down to a White House state dinner just hours after news that OpenAI had hacked the Australian government, we ask who will call to task the US tech titans at the table.

data.title: ‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating stroke
data.description: The Mercury prize winner hasn’t been able to go home since falling ill last summer. In his only interview, he opens up about the ‘poignancy’ of finally releasing the new album his stroke shelved At the end of July 2025, Michael Kiwanuka was back home in Southampton after a series of European gigs. His 2024 album Small Changes had been critically acclaimed and was kept off the UK No 1 slot only by Kendrick Lamar’s GNX. His fifth record, Fudge, was due that autumn. All was going perfectly for the virtuoso singer-songwriter, whose eccentric, genre-busting mix of psychedelic rock, prog soul, blues and gospel had marked him as a real one-off. Kiwanuka had been expected to appear at the All Together Now festival in County Waterford, Ireland, in the coming days, when an announcement was posted to his Instagram story: “We are so sorry to announce that due to continued illness, and on the advice of doctors, Michael will sadly be unable to perform at the rest of his scheduled festival performances throughout the rest of the summer and the shows in North America in October.” Continue reading...

data.title: Experience: a brain surgeon dropped part of my skull on the floor
data.description: I was a healthy 34-year-old when a mass of blood vessels ruptured in my brain. It took three neurosurgeons and a risky 16-hour operation to fix me On a Sunday in May 2017, I was at the gym and using a chest press when there was this pop. It wasn’t a sound – it was more like a sigh in my body. There was no pain, but I went limp. I shuffled along the wall to some mats. I thought I was having a stroke, but I wasn’t slurring and my eyes and arms seemed fine. But my left leg felt numb – it was the weirdest feeling. Lying on my back with my legs bent, both knees stayed upright when I looked at them. When I looked away, the left one fell to the side. I ended up in A&E for hours at nearby St Thomas’ hospital in London. I was 34, healthy and had started regaining feeling in my leg, so they theorised it was a bruised spine and thought it was safe to discharge me. Overworked staff and shift changes meant that when MRI images of my brain went missing, nobody tracked them down. Continue reading...

data.title: Berlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma Aydemir
data.description: Elif Eralp wants lower rents and more public housing. It’s not rocket science but mainstream parties still don’t get why they are failing Hope is a fragile thing. You can only hold on to it as long as you find reasons to believe tomorrow can be better. A woman, for instance, who has the resources and opportunity to rent her own flat will be more likely to leave her abusive husband and recover. A pupil who has their own room and desk to do their homework might find more meaning in thriving at school. And an elderly person who can afford to live in a neighbourhood where they feel safe and connected is less likely to become isolated and depressed. It’s not by chance that the examples above all revolve around the same topic. Affordable housing is possibly the most personal and most urgent social issue of our time. In Berlin, a city where 85% of residents live in rented accommodation, rents have risen by almost 70% in the past 10 years. And that is despite a rent control law that has been in effect since 2015. How? Loopholes and illegal practices have allowed property owners to continue putting pressure on the housing market. The social anxiety caused by this crisis, far from affecting just low-earners and single-parent households, affects vast parts of the middle class, too. Fatma Aydemir is a Berlin-based author, novelist, playwright and a Guardian Europe columnist Continue reading...

data.title: Ukraine war briefing: Finland urges Elon Musk to expand Kyiv’s Starlink coverage over Russia
data.description: Ukraine believes that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target missile launchers. What we know on day 1,675 Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside ⁠Russian territory. Ukraine ⁠has an acute shortage ​of air defences to repel Russian ballistic missiles and Kyiv believes that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the launchers that fire the missiles. Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over ‌Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine’s battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones, but it does not work over Russian territory. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has met with senior Wall Street executives on ​the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York , ⁠as Kyiv seeks to attract investments to help finance the country’s rebuilding efforts. The meeting focused mainly ⁠on areas such as helping Ukraine get through the winter and supporting its economy, the Ukrainian ⁠government said. Ukraine faces a brutal winter as stepped-up Russian strikes on ​its infrastructure and key ‌export industries deepen ‌the country’s budget crisis. The daily cost of the war ‌grew to about $190m this year. The meeting, attended by more than two dozen US companies, was facilitated by US banking giant Citigroup and the US chamber of commerce. Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said , in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services . In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia. The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”. Nato is capable of handling sabotage and drone incidents in Europe and has good action plans in place to deal with them , the alliance’s secretary general said after the warning from Danish intelligence. Secretary-general Mark Rutte said he believes the rising number of hybrid incidents in Nato countries shows that Russian President Vladimir Putin is losing the war in Ukraine. He said that citizens of the 32 Nato countries can remain calm. “Putin is in a bad place,” Rutte said. “He is not winning the war in Ukraine.” Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv and Ukraine’s north-east killed eight people on ⁠Thursday in attacks that included ⁠a maternity hospital and a ​farm , officials said. Two people died ⁠in the assault on Kyiv, Zelenskyy said. “As people were sleeping, flashes from explosions lit up the sky,” the president said on Telegram. Police said nine homes, a post office, ​warehouses and dozens of cars were also damaged in Kyiv. A separate ‌Russian attack on a vegetable storage ‌facility at a farm in a village of the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people and injured a further 12, prosecutors said. ⁠Turkish president Tayyip Erdogan said Turkey ⁠had ⁠stepped up ​efforts to re-establish the Black ⁠Sea grain corridor . “We have now increased ⁠our efforts to ​re-establish ‌the grain corridor. ‌We are also ‌accelerating our diplomatic steps for this,” Erdogan told a group of Turkish journalists ‌in New York. Erdogan said ⁠he had discussed ​the ​issue again ​with Zelenskyy ‌and received ​a ​positive response. Continue reading...

data.title: Ai Weiwei unveils his epic new Australian work: ‘90% of art is just garbage. Real art questions the existing order’
data.description: From his farm in Portugal, the acclaimed artist speaks about war, peace, the state of the world – and his 40 metre sculpture Mushrooms, on Sydney Harbour “It’s like a film set. Like it’s not real,” the bemused Uber driver says as we pass through a succession of silent rural villages washed with milky sunlight. He’s right: signs of human life are weirdly absent during our windy journey through the Alentejo. I’m making my way to Ai Weiwei’s secluded farm, nestled deep in the Portuguese countryside, where arguably the world’s best known living artist has quietly lived for the last six years. When I arrive, I am ushered inside a vast cathedral of a building, a replica of Ai’s erstwhile, and controversially demolished , studio in Shanghai. The space is cavernous. It’s gridded by huge wooden columns and its dizzyingly high ceilings are webbed with beams. There is no artwork on the walls, nor are there any obvious signs of production or activity. Continue reading...

data.title: Toys are us: the adults swapping scrolling for Lego, remote control cars and sewing
data.description: To escape the stresses and strains of adulting, more people are choosing to rekindle their love for childhood toys, games and pastimes A growing number of adult enthusiasts are rediscovering their love for Lego, helping to fuel a surge in sales that has increased the Danish toymaker’s revenues by 21%. But Lego isn’t the only childhood pastime people are returning to. We spoke to people who have rediscovered old hobbies about what drew them back. For some, returning to an old pastime offers an escape from the pressures of adult life, while for others it is a chance to reconnect with a younger version of themselves. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I have a blowtorch at uni’: what do students eat apart from pesto pasta?
data.description: Students are too broke or busy having fun to eat well, right? Wrong: some find cash and time for creme brulee and duck eggs This month marks 20 years since I arrived at university in London, with an Ikea saucepan set, a six-pack of Pot Noodle and a trusty jar of pesto to my name. I was a student now, and I intended to eat like one. But what did that mean? Where to my parents “student food” had hippyish connotations – lentils and ancient grains, communal pots of unidentifiable greige – by 2006 the stereotype had evolved to mean convenience and speed. Frozen pizza, potato waffles, mountains of pesto pasta – if we were eating at all, that is. As a 2000s girl with a 2000s diet mentality, I’ll admit that part of me hoped university would mark a turning point where I started having so much fun that I forgot to think about food. No such luck. What followed instead were probably the most formative eating years of my life; I don’t remember a single line of Beowulf, but those early tastes of independence are seared into my memory for ever. data.title: ‘My generation of novelists is dying’: Rose Tremain on 70 years of writing, and late-life inspiration
data.description: As her latest novel about Daphne du Maurier is published, the bestselling author reflects on age and creativity – and why at 83 she has no plans to stop My generation of writers is dying. Of Granta’s fabled list of 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, six are gone, including our most princely satirist, Martin Amis. We’re all approaching birthdays where the cake is too small for the candles. Some of us are wounded: Salman Rushdie by an attacker’s knife, Julian Barnes lives with blood cancer, others with the fatal hurt of being forgotten. But what’s the likely fate of those of us who are surviving – for now? Do readers still love us? When Barnes announced that he was signing off because of illness, was he also intuiting that the younger generations had heard enough from us old birds and geezers who were young when Sean Connery had dimples, when David Hockney first coloured his hair yellow? Continue reading...

data.title: My dad was a monster! Sara Karloff on reviving Frankenstein, 95 years on
data.description: Boris Karloff’s daughter and composer Michael Shapiro, whose musical score for the 1931 film is finally coming to London, talk about how it became a much-loved classic Once seen, never forgotten – the 1931 Frankenstein is 95 years old, but still one of the most instantly recognisable of classic horrors. Whether it’s the sight of lanky Boris Karloff lumbering into the frame with his squared-off head, neck bolts and oversized leaden shoes, or the sound of a thunderclap and Colin Clive exclaiming “It’s alive!” as the monster comes to life one stormy night in the laboratory – the film still raises hairs on the back of the neck. However, this classic has arguably long been missing one element: a continuous musical soundtrack – the original movie had dialogue but no music. In 2001, the American composer Michael Shapiro wrote a full-length score, which he will be conducting alongside the film for the first time in London next month, at Cadogan Hall with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. “It becomes one artistic expression, one artistic experience,” he says. “The film and the music, together, and the audience forgets that I am there.” Shapiro says his music emphasises what is already up on the screen. “Suddenly the film jumps out in a way it never did before.” Continue reading...

data.title: The lure of the loo: how restaurant bathroom design went wild
data.description: Plush or pared back, flatteringly lit or full-on disco camp, a TikTokkable loo is now part of the hospitality experience Anthony Bourdain was typically forthright when it came to his expectations for the toilet facilities in a food business. “I won’t eat in a restaurant with filthy bathrooms,” wrote the late chef and author, in his seminal, turn-of-the-millennium memoir Kitchen Confidential. “This isn’t a hard call. They let you see the bathrooms. If the restaurant can’t be bothered to replace the puck in the urinal or keep the toilets and floors clean, then just imagine what their refrigeration and work spaces look like.” Setting aside the fact that, in later life, Bourdain softened his stance (“Some of the best food experiences I’ve ever had [have been in] places where they really don’t give a shit [about bathroom cleanliness],” were his words in a 2018 interview) his initial take tells us plenty about what the average customer historically demanded of restaurant restrooms. They needed to be clean. They needed to be functional. They needed, at a push, half-decent hand soap and the faint, reassuring waft of pine-scented floor cleaner. Today, things could hardly be more different. Where once restaurant toilets tended to be a boring, unglamorous afterthought, in recent years, they have emerged as arguably the most unexpectedly attention-grabbing room in the building: atmospherically distinct sites of creativity and muscle-flexing design, where lavish amenities, bespoke lighting, custom soundscapes, selfie mirrors and all manner of other eye-catching flourishes abound, and are documented by social media channels, such as @LoosOfLondon (TikTok followers: 78k). Continue reading...

data.title: We all know a lack of exercise is bad for our bodies. So what is relying on AI doing to our brains? | Devi Sridhar
data.description: I suspect nearly all of my students use AI, and I worry about its corrosive effects. We must not entrust tech companies with our long-term health Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh When I was a postgraduate student at the University of Oxford in the early 2000s, I interviewed for a major consulting firm. All my friends were being recruited, and I thought why not give it a shot? Aside from the usual maths-proficiency test (how quickly can you crunch numbers in front of a client and look smart), I was asked about what the future of streaming could look like. I gave a long-winded answer about the unintended consequences of changing how humans interact with each other when a new technology is introduced, and why this may not be in the best interests of health and society. I even remember saying something like: “Can you imagine just being stuck at home, alone, watching show after show and never having to move or see any other people? Why would anyone choose that over going out to rent a DVD at a local shop, or to a movie theatre?” You won’t be surprised to learn that I wasn’t invited for a follow-up interview. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

data.title: Plans are under way to finally help Britain’s unemployed young people – will Labour pull it off? | Polly Toynbee
data.description: Alan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it through As certainly as the moon pulls on the tides, Labour governments improve the lives of the poorest children. Just as surely, Conservative governments pull back and reverse the good done. Here we go again: despite the social devastation caused by George Osborne’s cuts last time, Kemi Badenoch announces that she wants to impose cuts to universal credit for the poorest if she gets the chance. She doesn’t do subtle, none of Iain Duncan Smith’s cruel-to-be-kind routine, but goes straight for populist rabble-rousing, stirring up fact-free contempt for anyone on benefits, with a proposed ban on buying cigarettes and alcohol, or gambling, with benefit money. Welfare, she says, must not be “a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered”. As with all crude rightwing populism, the harm she does spreads hatred of the weak. In this most unequal country, it encourages bullies to kick downwards, stifling more generous human instincts. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

data.title: Open AI attacked Australia’s health system – and then doubled down on its negligence. The time for ‘wait and see’ is over | Kate Crawford and Edward Santow
data.description: Human hackers face serious consequences, and so must AI companies. There is no excuse for what happened Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast When you get sick, Medicare exists to take care of you. It sits at the centre of a health system that our prime minister rightly calls the envy of the world . It’s one of the few institutions nearly every Australian still trusts. So when an AI company threatens this system, it couldn’t be more serious. We are at the UN general assembly this week and the OpenAI hack has put Australia in the spotlight during an expanding cybersecurity crisis. World leaders are calling for stronger oversight of frontier models. We know Medicare must be secure or our doctors and hospitals cannot do their jobs. But this breach is also a test of something larger: whether the Australian government can hold a US tech giant to account when its technology goes rogue. If Australia can’t protect our community – if it can’t enforce our laws and prevent such attacks happening again – then we are entering a terrifying period. Continue reading...

data.title: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial
data.description: Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high. The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger . Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February , from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating. Continue reading...

data.title: De la Fuente brings insatiable Spain to England knowing World Cup is not enough
data.description: Spain have won back-to-back major tournaments, but there is still one more to go to draw equal with feted team of 2008-2012 “I’m going to tell you a story,” Luis de la Fuente said. “As soon as the game finished on 19 July, before anyone had cooled down at all, just two or three minutes after the final, one of the players – and you’ll have to forgive me for not telling you which one, but it was one of those who has been with us for the longest time – came up to me and said: ‘ Mister , now what? What’s left to win?’ And I said: ‘Bloody hell, the game against England at Wembley on 26 September.’” It was a Friday afternoon at Las Rozas and Spain’s coach had just named his first squad since that day in New Jersey . It was a familiar one, full of history makers. Of the 26 from the World Cup, only four had been left out and there was an explanation for each: Marcos Llorente has announced his international retirement; Joan García is injured; Borja Iglesias, who always felt the likeliest to leave first, is not fully fit; and Gavi is suspended for Wembley, although he could have faced Croatia and Czechia. Continue reading...

data.title: João Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flat
data.description: There was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the kingdom of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, the cue to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket of Wales supporters. The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and his disallowed goal, after skating offside to latch on to a Bruno Fernandes pass. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to the locals who worship him. Continue reading...

data.title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’
data.description: Two years ago the Brazilian thought his time at Barcelona was ending but, two La Liga titles later, he is now captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere. There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best. Continue reading...

data.title: Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worth
data.description: The Ryder Cup-style event has struggled financially since its legendary founder, Roger Federer, retired but still offers a spectacle unlike any other in tennis The sight of a tennis player marching to the bathroom between sets has become increasingly common in modern tennis but Alexander Zverev’s journey back to the locker room in Prague nine years ago remains particularly remarkable. On this occasion, Zverev happened to be sandwiched between two of the greatest male players of all time. Neither legend was happy. To his right, an incensed Roger Federer spent their walk back to the locker room brutally laying down the law: “I want a fist pump or a ‘Let’s go!’ every fucking point you win,” he said. “And every point you lose, you fucking take it like a man. Because the problem is, when you don’t have the [result] you want, it’s like: ‘Ah, I knew it. Fuck, shit.’ I don’t want … honestly!” Continue reading...

data.title: Leaders join push to create UN body to tackle ‘awful reality’ of inequality
data.description: Body would be modelled on climate panel and recognise inequality as a global challenge threatening world security Plans to set up a global UN body on inequality modelled on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) are likely to be proposed to a meeting of the UN general assembly in the coming months. Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the general assembly in New York, left-leaning leaders from Brazil, Norway and Spain claimed momentum was building behind calls for a standing international panel on inequality that would recognise the issue as a global challenge threatening world security. Two G7 countries – Germany and Japan – have given public backing. Continue reading...

data.title: Would you bet on the future of our planet?
data.description: Prediction markets are focusing on extreme weather and the climate crisis. But it’s led to questions about what exactly people are betting on • Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here How hot will it get in your nearest city tomorrow? How quickly will the planet’s ice melt and its corals die off? How many huge, costly climate disasters will hit this year? If you’re inclined to do so, you can now place online bets on how the weather and the broader, longer-term climate crisis will play out. Kalshi recently reported 500% growth in weather and climate wagers over the past year, taking the market to a $1.1bn, and is now partnering with the Weather Company, which owns the Weather Channel, to boost its credibility in this new arena. data.title: Africa’s universities need overhaul to harness continent’s young talent, says public health expert
data.description: Dr John Nkengasong, a former WHO adviser who worked with Biden administration on Aids policy, says decolonising curriculums and investment are key to unlocking potential of continent’s graduates African governments need to shake off the legacy of colonialism and underfunding if their education systems are ever to harness the vast potential of the continent’s young talent, says the public health expert Dr John Nkengasong. Africa’s young demographic – it is the world’s youngest continent with 70% of people aged under 30 – is seen as its greatest asset . But a lack of cohesion between education institutions and employers means graduates in Africa, whose number is rising, are not well prepared when they start work, Nkengasong says. In an interview with the Guardian, he says students should be primed to address the continent’s socioeconomic problems, whether through influencing public health policy or technological innovation. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I never choose the cautious option’: Royal Opera’s Jakub Hrůša on collaboration, control and conducting Wagner
data.description: One year into the role, the Royal Opera’s music director is taking on the challenge of Parsifal, and, next season, the Ring Cycle. I’m here, and I am courageous says the conductor ‘You can choose the cautious option – or you can take the full risk and just go and conduct. Maybe I would like the cautious option, but I never choose it.” Jakub Hrůša learned to trust his instincts at the Royal Opera House back in 2022 when he conducted his first ever Wagner opera – Lohengrin – there, describing the experience as “one of the absolute highlights of my life”. Now he’s a year into his role as the house’s music director and about to conduct his first Parsifal, staged by Evgeny Titov. And next season there’ll be yet more Wagner firsts when he conducts complete cycles of the Ring as staged by Barrie Kosky . For most conductors, this would be a gradual process, adding the four Ring operas to their repertoire one by one, but not for Hrůša: he’ll be conducting his first Das Rheingold, Die Walküre, Siegfried and Götterdämmerung all in the space of a week. “Is it too bold? I find it wonderful!” he says. “I could have chosen to do it in my own way, in 10 years’ time, somewhere else – but I’m here, I’m the music director, the Ring should be done and wants to be done in its entirety, and I am courageous.” Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I get lost going to the bathroom’: John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being ‘the Scottish Eminem’
data.description: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on being confused with James Nesbitt, his own Sliding Doors moment and a new perspective since turning 60 How often do you get asked to recite that WH Auden poem from Four Weddings and a Funeral , and can you do it from memory right now? mattyjj and simoit Not for a long time. I could probably do the first couple of lines: Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone / Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone / Turn out the lights? And with muffled drums / Something, something … let the mourners come. There you go. Terrible! In Steve Coogan ’s Paul Calf’s Video Diary, your character praises Orson Welles’ The Trial for its “tremendous energy”, while Paul says he would “rather watch Dave Lee Travis playing Macbeth”. What’s your actual opinion of The Trial [by Franz Kafka]? AdrianH1 God, it’s a long time since I’ve read that. I read a lot of those books in my younger days, but probably, like a lot of people, even those who are graduates of English literature, I’d be hard pushed these days to tell you what it was about, other than the persecution of some minor character. data.title: Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?
data.description: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks It may not be quite as politically buzzy as the price of gasoline or eggs, but another household expense is going up for millions of people. Disney has brought the price-gouging experience of its theme park home again by raising the prices of most iterations and bundles of its Disney+ and Hulu streaming services. Whether you pay to watch them with or without ads, separately or bundled together, you’re probably getting a price hike of a couple of bucks per month. The few bundles that will remain the same price feature ad-supported versions of both services (plus ESPN). Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic! This particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has a dedicated page aggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner. Continue reading...

data.title: East of Eden to Kill Jackie: the seven best shows to stream this week
data.description: Florence Pugh shines as the icy sociopath at the heart of the Steinbeck classic, plus Catherine Zeta-Jones plays an international cocaine dealer in a truly bananas thriller “A girl like that doesn’t just fall out of the sky.” Charles Trask has a bad feeling about Cathy Ames, the woman who has arrived, beaten almost to death, on the doorstep of the farm he shares with his brother Adam. But it’s too late – Adam is smitten and therefore doomed. Zoe Kazan is behind this adaptation of John Steinbeck’s study of family, free will and arbitrary evil. data.title: Jae Stephens: Audacity review – a thrilling lesson in why more debut albums should go for broke
data.description: (Def Jam) After five EPs in in seven years, the Dallas native with the big voice pours everything into this bonkers cauldron of maximalist R&B and hyperactive pop There is so, so much happening on Jae Stephens’ debut album Audacity. Thankfully, it seems like mess is her medium. Although the 29-year-old Dallas native is often sold as a big voice – and she undoubtedly does have a big voice – her debut album has more in common with hyperactive, magnetic records such as PinkPantheress’s Fancy That or Salute’s True Magic: recent albums whose need for speed and sweetly toned maximalism fostered an irrepressible sense of personality. Stephens is an apt case study of a career in the contemporary pop industry: she started writing, producing and performing alone in her room, and dropped a whopping five EPs in the seven years before Audacity’s release. She has written with a host of pop also-rans and, inexplicably, hosts a music interview podcast. But listening to Audacity forces me into that age-old cliche: why isn’t this artist a bigger star? Continue reading...

data.title: Norma Tanega and Aida Pavletich: Saturday Dancer review | Safi Bugel's experimental album of the month
data.description: (Freedom to Spend) Far from her conventional 60s and 70s hits, Tanega joined up with a friend for an endearingly eccentric ‘rap opera’ spanning swampy synths and sardonic showtunes Perhaps you know Norma Tanega for her chirpy 60s folk pop, such as Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog, which charted in the US and Canada. Or perhaps you know her swooning ballads from the 70s, which have had a streaming-aided resurgence in popularity. Lesser known are her wonky, nocturnal keyboard and drum machine experiments, recorded between the late 80s and early 90s with friend and writer Aida Pavletich. Together, the pair produced a trio of tapes on a four-track in Tanega’s home studio, which are now being reissued. The first of the three, Saturday Dancer, is billed as a “rap opera”, which gives a sense of the album’s theatrical tone, if not the genre. Over 19 scuzzy and shapeshifting vignettes, the duo narrate a noirish night out on the town, from stripteases and sticky tables to the dread that seeps in when the lights come on – with some frankly bizarre tangents. The lo-fi instrumentals are suitably delirious, with clattering, likely improvised percussion and eerie synths lurking somewhere between strange and seductive. Continue reading...

data.title: The rise of Dom Dolla: what the DJ’s record-breaking stadium show for 60,000 fans tells us about music today
data.description: Dom Dolla’s enormous show in Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium set a new record for a solo EDM artist in Australia, and proves how the genre is dominating “Abandon all hope, ye who enter,” it says on the wall – no, my mistake, that is just the sign for the Johnnie Walker bar at Marvel Stadium. I have a theory that what everyone is drinking at a show can tell you a lot about the mood of a crowd, and based on the stacks of Hard Solo and Walker cans strewn on the streets outside Dom Dolla’s biggest ever show, 60,000 people are in for an intense, sticky night. And a significant one. That 60,000 people have turned out to see a DJ play in a stadium, the biggest electronic dance music (EDM) concert by a solo artist ever staged in Australia’s history, tells us something about the way music is changing – both in Australia and outside it. data.title: Honegger: Jeanne d’Arc au Bûcher album review – faultless recording of an eclectic masterpiece
data.description: Bonnet/Dutrieux/Czech Philharmonic/Vasilek (Animal Music) Honegger’s multifaceted 1935 composition about the French saint is brought to life in spine-tingling detail by Lukáš Vasilek, the Czech Philharmonic and  actors and musicians Honegger’s Jeanne d’Arc au Bûcher is a neglected masterpiece. Composed in 1935 to a text by Paul Claudel, it reviews the French saint’s life in flashback as she awaits execution. Eleven episodes explore her physical and mental trials, with actors playing Jeanne and her confidant Frère Dominique alongside a cast of solo singers and full chorus. Honegger’s score blends medieval modes and folk melody with Stravinskian neoclassicism and jazz, while his eclectic orchestration includes three saxophones, pianos and the eerie wail of the ondes Martenot. This new recording gets everything right. Lukáš Vasilek directs the Czech Philharmonic in a dramatically nuanced and scrupulously engineered account. Set pieces land body blows. Jeanne’s examination before a tribunal of anthropomorphic animals sizzles with faux-Hollywood fanfares and a scabrous comedic energy. Kyle van Schoonhoven has fun as Porcus, the pig elected to preside over her trial. The game of cards, where blase English and French nobility use her as a bargaining chip, is razor-sharp. The Prague Philharmonic Choir and Children’s Choir are splendidly muscular. Hovering over it all are Jeanne’s otherworldly voices – the Virgin, Sainte Catherine and Sainte Marguerite – captured here in spine-tingling detail. Continue reading...

data.title: Can’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius?
data.description: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon ‘There’s an anxiety in declaring oneself a Kylie fan,” wrote the late San Francisco poet Kevin Killian (who nonetheless once published an entire collection devoted to the singer). Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmament has often felt more precarious than that of other artists, perhaps because of her past as a soap star, and the schmaltz of some of her early material with Stock Aitken Waterman. But she has always displayed a canny self-awareness, alongside a willingness to push the envelope. It’s evident in her knowing rendition of I Should Be So Lucky as a bad poem at the Royal Albert Hall in 1996, and her many collaborations with experimental dance producers. Then there’s her instinct for giving fans what they want: inarguable bangers, like those of her 2000s imperial phase, that also possess an offbeat, idiosyncratic quality, true of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and of her 2023 viral hit, Padam Padam. Continue reading...

data.title: Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty review – Big Little Lies sequel shoots for high drama but fails to deliver
data.description: At 400-plus pages, Moriarty’s follow-up is too long and offers too little reward, with menopause, vaping teens and even a stalker failing to raise the stakes Liane Moriarty’s Big Little Lies was such a runaway success – debuting at No 1 on the New York Times bestseller list and adapted for a television miniseries starring Reese Witherspoon, Nicole Kidman and Zoë Kravitz – that she always had her work cut out for her if she was to return the fluctuating narrative back to the page. Recognising this hurdle, Moriarty opens the sequel (her first) with a note to readers that details the way the new novel both responds to its TV adaptation – by making Laura Dern’s Renata and Meryl Streep’s Mary-Louise more central characters – and returns readers to the original landscape, the fictional Pirriwee Peninsula along Sydney’s northern beaches. Moriarty immediately situates the reader back in Australia: a magpie swoops “like a missile” at an unsuspecting cyclist against a backdrop of “bright yellow native wattle” and “lush-purple” jacarandas. Time has passed, in both the real and fictional world. It has been 12 years since the 2014 publication of Big Little Lies, and the sweet kindergarteners at the heart of the original are teenagers now, with mothers in the midst of menopause. The idyllic setting is shattered when a severed human finger is posted to the local high school, setting the scene for a sequel packed with all the intrigue, drama and suspense of the first. Continue reading...

data.title: Turner prize review – soulful cyborgs go into battle with a stack of massive Hobnobs
data.description: Mima, Middlesbrough In a truly competitive year, Kira Freije’s apocalyptic humanoids trounce everything in their path, even the sculpture that looks like a pile of biscuits The Turner prize is most exciting when you passionately support one of the artists and want to convince everyone she’s a genius. In this year’s show at Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art, I felt that thrill so strongly, I want to get a T-shirt made to support my artist like the Boro scarves and banners you see around here. Kira Freije has her own floor, separated by a tall flight of stairs from the three other shortlisted artists, because apparently the fine watery mist in her installation could damage their fragile materials. Yet setting her apart seems like a statement and it’s justified. She shows 33 lifesize statues of tragicomic steampunk cyborgs, individual works but gathered in a vaporous apocalyptic wasteland, with an impact and resonance that’s on a level of its own. data.title: Nicole Eisenman review – ICE-like goons clash with sublime stargazing as America’s magical magpie returns
data.description: Sadie Coles HQ, London Abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the ground Nicole Eisenman’s 2023 exhibition at the Whitechapel Gallery took its title from Hillary Clinton’s account of the 2016 US presidential election: “What happened.” With its absurdist riffs on contemporary American life, the show confirmed that Eisenman is among the most important artists of her time and that “what happened” was a disaster. So her return to London might be thought of as a sequel, with the working title: “So what do we do now?” Eisenman is justly celebrated for her rambunctious, magpie and irreverent subversions of the conventional histories of art and society. A painter who has lately (and successfully) turned to sculpture, her work often places people in situations – ranging from crowded bars to town squares flooded with mud – that match broad humour to sharp technique in reflecting on how our identities are shaped by the company we keep. And yet my first thought on entering Sadie Coles’ gallery was the artist had turned her back on the world. Continue reading...

data.title: Do any coffee-flavoured drinks come close to the real thing?
data.description: In which a UK coffee lover, long devoted to her moka pot, tiptoes gingerly into the world of coffee-derived drink products My family has benefited hugely from charities that support healthcare , so it is with extra zeal that I’ll be drinking coffee with a slice of cake tomorrow to mark this year’s Macmillan Coffee Morning . In anticipation, I’ve been tasting some coffee-flavoured drinks. I should preface this by saying that, when it comes to coffee, I am a creature of habit and, almost 30 years into my relationship with the stuff, I know what I like: short-ish, strong, preferably made in a moka pot and only a tiny splash of milk. I’m less faithful to brands, though I do rate Union’s House Roast , which is bold, crowdpleasing, not too bitter and sold in most big supermarkets. Much as my partner has tried to seduce me to the trendy charms of filter coffee, this leopard can’t seem to change her spots. Continue reading...

data.title: What to cook when summer meets autumn
data.description: The weather is in transition, so here are some dishes to bridge the gap between crisp salads and hearty stews Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast The weather in London can’t quite make up its mind. You leave the house in the morning and immediately wish you’d brought gloves, but by lunchtime you’re carrying your jacket under your arm, and by dinner you’re closing the windows again. Summer hasn’t exactly gone, but winter has started sending little reminders that it knows where we live. We love this time of year. The air feels fresh from the occasional shower, the days are still long enough to make something of, the light is perhaps the most beautiful it will be all year, and, for cycling, it is perfect. There are days when London seems to contain two seasons at once: summer in a sunny spot at lunchtime, winter the moment the sun disappears. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Going places with panache’: Max Mara channels audacious women for Milan show
data.description: Chore jackets and loose-fit trousers nod to ‘nonconformist glamour’ of Amelia Earhart and other pioneers The Max Mara catwalk at Milan fashion week had well-cut coats, sturdy block-heeled boots, crisp white shirts and capacious suede handbags. What it quite deliberately did not have was shock value. “I hope everyone watching this show can recognise something of themselves in what they see,” said Ian Griffiths, the British designer who has been at this Italian house since 1987. “I think that’s really important. Without being critical of other brands or designers, so much of fashion alienates people and makes them feel that they aren’t good enough or thin enough or young enough to wear what’s being represented.” Trousers were pleated and roomy, skirts long enough to be elegant but not long enough to trip you up. In shades of sand and chalk, grey and black, every piece was designed to work with everything else, and to blend into an existing wardrobe. The styling gestures – a popped collar here, a knotted belt there – stopped short of gimmick. The models could have walked off the runway and on to the Milan street – which, Griffiths said backstage, was the point. “The catwalk show is only the prelude to what to me is the real presentation, which is when I see women walking down the street in my clothes.” Continue reading...

data.title: Toxic bosses: why do companies protect managers who make working life hell?
data.description: Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top. How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel? When Andrea finally resigned, her colleagues told her the truth they had always known about her boss. Some apologised. Others admitted they had watched what happened to her and said nothing. One offered the sentence I have been unable to forget: “You’ve been an emotional stab vest for us. You protected us.” Andrea was a senior legal executive with decades of credibility when she began reporting to a powerful new colleague. Within months, something was wrong. Expectations shifted without warning and feedback contradicted itself. He spoke over her in public and undermined her in private. Slowly she began questioning not just him but herself, her competence, even her grip on reality. Continue reading...

data.title: Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against Germany
data.description: At least Germany can be sure it will not be dull. Jürgen Klopp had predicted his debut as head coach could be wild, a trait he would accept as long as his team were lively enough. Both transpired in a frayed, pinball-like game whose lack of quality could be forgiven on account of its entertainment levels. The Netherlands more than merited a brilliant late equaliser from Cody Gakpo and by the time those present had drawn breath it felt appropriate that, for all the talk of new dawns, everyone finished back where they had started. World domination is a far-off prospect for both of these flailing giants on such scrappy, frenetic evidence. But at least those with a stake in this famous old fixture, largely shorn of the spite and spit that defined it of old, could come away feeling something. Restoring those essential sensations of joy, pain and meaning sits at the very top of Klopp’s priorities. Germany looked raw and scattergun for long periods, reined in only by their lack of technical aptitude, but there were signs of an energy that had long been missing. Continue reading...

data.title: 51,000 reclining chair batteries recalled after reports of fires
data.description: The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission has recalled approximately 51,000 lithium-ion battery packs from Blue Cactus Company. Proper disposal methods are required due to the fire hazard associated with these batteries.

This passionate advocate plans to distribute more bracelets this Halloween, continuing her mission.

data.title: Massachusetts restores cranberry bog to protect rare trout that moves between river and ocean
data.description: Massachusetts is restoring Century Bog, a former cranberry farm in Plymouth and Wareham, to complete protection of Red Brook from White Island Pond to Buttermilk Bay. The restored wetland and stream channel could benefit about 60 conservation-priority species, including “salter” brook trout that move between freshwater and saltwater estuaries.

data.title: Why is Finland asking Musk to help Ukraine prepare for winter war against Russia?
data.description: Russian ballistic missile strikes reached record levels this summer, putting further pressure on Ukraine's already limited air defence resources. Patriot systems are currently the only Ukrainian air defences capable of intercepting such missiles, but Kyiv's stocks of interceptor missiles are severely depleted. Musk activated Starlink over Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

data.title: DN Debatt. ”Oja er inte över lokala partier – de fyller en viktig funktion”

data.title: Over extreem weer kan Nederland nog veel leren van landen in Afrika: ‘Hier kijken we naar civieltechnische maatregelen, in veel andere landen gebruiken ze natuurlijke oplossingen’
data.description: Wat kan Nederland leren van Afrika en Azië over de aanpak bij extreem weer? In Zuid-Limburg, dat vijf jaar geleden werd getroffen door zware regenval en overstromingen, werken het Wereld Natuur Fonds en het Rode Kruis samen in een project dat ervaringen uit andere landen naar Nederland brengt.

data.title: Verkoudheid is een vastberaden doorzetter
data.description: Frits Abrahams is verkouden. Dat gebeurt hem twee keer per jaar. Dus honderdvijftig keer tot nu toe! Toch laat hij zich elke keer door het virus verrassen. En denkt hij ten onrechte: deze keer valt het wel mee. Verkoudheden plaatsen je voor een lastig sociaal dilemma. Mag je de geliefde die je een poosje niet hebt gezien nog pardoes kussen?

data.title: Opravy trvají věčnost. Chceme tým, co závady vyřeší hned, říká lídr Richard Matiašek
data.description: Lídr uskupení Zdraví Sport Vzdělání Richard Matiašek cílí v Ústí nad Labem na sedm až deset procent hlasů. Pro městské obvody žádá desítky milionů navíc na opravy chodníků či osvětlení. V předvolebním rozhovoru vysvětluje, proč je nutné zrychlit údržbu města, jak chce zvýšit bezpečnost obyvatel i proč současnému magistrátu vázne komunikace s lidmi.

data.title: Trump řekl, že povolí Ukrajině vyrábět střely do systémů Patriot, uvedl Zelenskyj
data.description: Ukrajinský prezident Volodymyr Zelenskyj oznámil, že mu šéf Bílého domu Donald Trump na jejich schůzce tento týden řekl, že Spojené státy Ukrajině povolí vyrábět střely do systémů protivzdušné obrany Patriot. Ukrajina, na kterou Rusko opakovaně útočí balistickými raketami, se potýká s akutním nedostatkem střel do svých obranných systémů.

data.title: V Turecku havaroval minibus s turisty, mezi 17 zraněnými je i Češka
data.description: Sedmnáct lidí včetně jedné české turistky utrpělo zranění při dopravní nehodě v turecké provincii Antalya. Turistický minibus se střetl s dvěma dalšími vozy, načež přerazil sloup semaforu a převrátil se na bok. Několik lidí skončilo v nemocnici, ale nejsou v ohrožení života.

data.title: V Soči dokončili přestavbu Putinova sídla. Kvůli útokům tam ale přestal jezdit
data.description: V jihoruském Soči finišuje přestavba rezidence diktátora Vladimira Putina. Zakázku bez výběrového řízení dostala na starost firma napojená na jeho přítele, která pro šéfa Kremlu stavěla v minulosti i na okupovaném Krymu. Stavaře společnost rekrutovala na sociálních sítích a nalákala třeba na ubytovnu s bazénem. Kolem celého objektu roste také neprostupná bezpečností zóna, jež zásadně ovlivní život v okolí.

data.title: Vládu čeká hlasování o nedůvěře, Babiš se těší. Krade budoucnost, řekl Kupka
data.description: Vládu Andreje Babiše čeká necelé dva týdny před senátními a komunálními volbami hlasování o nedůvěře. Vyvolat se ho rozhodla parlamentní opozice, která má pro vyvolání hlasování o nedůvěře 92 podpisů poslanců. Premiér Babiš reagoval, že se na schůzi těší. Občané si podle něj zaslouží vědět pravdu, když musí poslouchat lži opozice. Mimořádná schůze před hlasováním začne v úterý 29. září.

data.title: Obec kvůli banalitě skončila v exekuci. Starostka za chybu zaplatila desítky tisíc
data.description: Z běžné žádosti o informace se stal spor, který skončil až exekucí obce. Loučná nad Desnou na Šumpersku neposkytla developerovi informace týkající se připravované změny územního plánu ani poté, co jí povinnost uložil soud. Starostka Petra Harazímová pochybení přiznává a tvrdí, že vzniklé náklady zaplatila ze svého.

data.title: Zoo Praha oslaví 95. výročí. Přijďte v kostýmu ze 30. let a nechte si vytvořit účes z té doby
data.description: Od prvního otevření pražské zoo uplyne v pondělí 28. září 95 let. Právě odkazem na 30. léta se zahrada rozhodla své narozeniny oslavit a pro návštěvníky připravila speciální program. Nebudou chybět historická vozidla, dobové kostýmy, hudební či taneční vystoupení. Zájemcům kadeřníci zdarma vytvoří také dobový účes.

data.title: Padesátiletí U2 mají zase radost. Na novém albu zazní naposledy hlas Dolly Partonové
data.description: Bylo to 25. září 1976 v irském Dublinu, kdy se čtveřice Bono, The Edge, Larry Mullen Jr. a Adam Clayton začala sypat na hromadu první společné hudební nápady. Po padesáti letech jsou U2 jednou z největších světových kapel a snad i k oslavám narozenin potěší 13. listopadu fanoušky dlouho slibovanou albovou novinkou Carnaval De Luz.

data.title: AfD chce jednat o návratu ruského plynu do Německa. Ve hře je i Nord Stream
data.description: Německá Alternativa pro Německo (AfD) a ekonomický zmocněnec ruského prezidenta Vladimira Putina Kirill Dmitrijev připravují schůzku, na níž chtějí jednat o obnovení dodávek ruského plynu do Německa. Setkání by se mohlo uskutečnit už v březnu příštího roku a mezi diskutovanými tématy má být také případné znovuotevření plynovodů Nord Stream.

data.description: Před čtyřmi lety byl Jiří Robenek lídrem kandidátky Pirátů ve Zlíně. Teď je jím opět. Přesto je však v jiné pozici. Založil hnutí Zlín srdcem, které s Piráty vytvořilo společnou kandidátku, na níž jsou i nestraníci. Důvodem byl fakt, že nebyl spokojený s vedením Pirátů.

data.title: Batthyány znovu primátorem? Liberec strašně usnul a chátrá, říká lídr Libe!
data.description: Tibor Batthyány vedl Liberec jako primátor do roku 2018. Po osmi letech se rozhodl opět kandidovat, tentokrát jako lídr politického uskupení Libe! data.title: Okoun v krustě, Musk a pompa. Ale jinak schůzka Trumpa se Siem nic nepřinesla
data.description: Americký prezident Donald Trump ve čtvrtek přivítal v Bílém domě svůj čínský protějšek Si Ťin-pchinga na okázalém summitu, jenž byl bohatý na symboliku, ale chudý na obsah, napsala agentura Reuters. Konkrétní výsledky schůzka nepřinesla a nenaznačila ani průlom v citlivých otázkách, jako jsou umělá inteligence, vzájemný obchod, Tchaj-wan či válka s Íránem.

data.title: Macinka se v New Yorku zaměřil na Afriku. Politolog vysvětlil, co může Česku přinést
data.description: Ministr zahraničí Petr Macinka se v New Yorku zaměřil zejména na setkání se zástupci afrických zemí. „Relativně malou investicí politického času lze získat mnoho,“ vysvětlil pro iDNES.cz. „Afrika je rozlehlá, lidnatá, bohatá na suroviny. To všechno jsou věci, které ve světě vždy měly váhu,“ doplnil pro iDNES.cz politický geograf Michael Romancov a vysvětlil výhody regionu i možné ambice České republiky.

data.title: Ukrajinci poškodili rafinerii Lukoilu. Rusko v Kyjevě zasáhlo věžáky, zemřel chlapec

data.title: Zásadní je zrychlit dobu oprav silnic, říká brněnský lídr Motoristů

Strana, která loni poprvé pronikla do Poslanecké sněmovny a následně se dokonce stala součástí vlády, sází hlavně na dlouholetého starostu Bystrce Tomáše Kratochvíla. data.title: NATO by mohlo vytvořit letku proti dronům. Analytik vidí vhodný stroj v českém Skyfoxu
data.description: Severoatlantická aliance (NATO) by mohla vytvořit mnohonárodní letku specializovanou na zachycování a ničení útočných dronů, která by umožnila šetřit drahé bojové letouny a zásoby raket vzduch-vzduch. Za jednu z nejvhodnějších platforem pro takovou jednotku považuje expert z britského Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) Justin Bronk český proudový letoun L-39NG Skyfox vyráběný společností Aero Vodochody. Uvedl to ve své analýze.

data.title: Houbařské žně? Úrodu mohou překazit mrazíky. Mykoložka radí, na co si dát pozor
data.description: Houbařská sezona je v Česku v plném proudu. O prodlouženém víkendu mohou lidé v lesích narazit na smrkové i hnědé hřiby, klouzky, kozáky nebo křemenáče. Situace se ale může podle aktuální předpovědi počasí výrazně změnit. „Hlásí přízemní mrazíky. Ty by mohly růst hub zpomalit i úplně zastavit,“ říká v rozhovoru pro iDNES.cz mykoložka Tereza Tejklová.

data.title: Rescatistas venezolanos que actuaron en La Guaira y Colombia: El tiempo no se mide igual cuando alguien espera debajo de una estructura
data.description: Después de participar en las operaciones de respuesta a los sismos en La Guaira (Venezuela) y Pereira (Colombia), Jordy González y Víctor Dávila, del Grupo de Rescate Domingo Peña de Mérida,  comparten un análisis sobre las diferencias operativas en ambos escenarios. La experiencia permitió contrastar dos realidades de gestión de emergencias: mientras que en Venezuela los rescatistas enfrentaron condiciones marcadas por la precariedad y la improvisación logística, en el país vecino se integraron a un sistema de gestión de riesgo altamente organizado. The post Rescatistas venezolanos que actuaron en La Guaira y Colombia: El tiempo no se mide igual cuando alguien espera debajo de una estructura appeared first on EL NACIONAL .

data.title: "Es como si te borraran toda tu vida": sobrevivientes de los terremotos afrontan la incertidumbre de volver a empezar
data.description: Aricel Bravo, Alejandro Ferrería, Joanna González y Mayuri Calderín sobrevivieron al doble terremoto del 24 de junio, pero perdieron sus viviendas y, con ellas, buena parte de rutinas que sostenían sus vidas. Algunos edificios ya fueron demolidos y otros esperan una decisión. Mientras el Estado anuncia créditos para adquirir nuevas propiedades, las familias resuelven alquileres, mudanzas, colegios, empleos alterados y la incertidumbre de no saber dónde estarán en los próximos meses. data.description:
En l’espace d’une semaine, chaque colline devra avoir recensé les besoins individuels en engrais, a annoncé le président Évariste Ndayishimiye le 17 septembre 2026 à Gitega. Face aux difficultés d’approvisionnement et aux soupçons de détournement, des experts préconisent la dépolitisation du secteur et le retrait des autorités de la distribution des fertilisants.

Par Jules Bercy Igiraneza et Félix Haburiyakira

data.description: Before dawn broke on September 9, 2026, the Maino family’s PMV truck rolled out of Inawi village in the Mekeo Kuni Rural LLG of Kairuku District, Central Province. Bound for Port Moresby, its cargo was familiar bags of green betelnut harvested directly from the family plantation. For 25-year-old George Maino, this was no ordinary trip. While his brothers and sister pursued higher education in the city funded by their parents’ decades of hard work in the betelnut trade, George was the son who chose to stay back. data.title: Affaire des lunettes du ministre : L’UDC exige des excuses publiques et réparation pour les quatre journalistes humiliés
data.description: © DR L'affaire des quatre journalistes interpellés pour le vol présumé des lunettes du ministre de l’Economie, de la Planification et de l’Aménagement du Territoire Alamine Ousmane Mey prend une tournure politique. L’UDC y voit une autre forme d’atteinte à la démocratie. Dans une déclaration officielle signée de son président national, le maire Hermine Patricia Tomaino Ndam Njoya, l'Union démocratique du Cameroun (UDC) ne mâche pas ses mots. Elle exige clairement la réparation du préjudice subi par les journalistes ainsi que des excuses publiques. Pour le parti du regretté Adamou Ndam Njoya, l'incident survenu les 16 et 17 septembre 2026 en marge des Journées de la Banque islamique de développement au Palais des Congrès est "aussi insolite que fâcheux, car des plus dégradant". L'Union démocratique du Cameroun se demande comment on peut comprendre que des journalistes en plein exercice de leur métier soient confondus avec de vulgaires voleurs. Qu'ils soient à la va-vite aussi facilement jetés en cellule et à la vindicte populaire. La formation politique rappelle le fait le plus accablant : selon les déclarations des victimes, les lunettes auraient été retrouvées dès le 17 septembre à l'intérieur même du véhicule du ministre, alors que les journalistes François Essomba, Igor Gwet Bibey, Solange Djuikam et Pierre Mouchili sont restés en garde à vue au commissariat central n°1 jusqu'au 21 septembre, dans des "conditions de tristes renommées". Dénonçant un tel traitement, le parti énonce cinq exigences : il rappelle que la presse, Quatrième pouvoir, mérite considération. S’indigne de la "clochardisation de nos Médias" par le régime. Réaffirme son engagement pour une presse fière et libre. Exprime sa désolation aux quatre victimes. Et surtout, demande que réparation soit faite et que des excuses publiques soient présentées. La position de l’UDC qui rejoint celle du Syndicat national des professionnels de l’information et de la communication –SPIC- qui, reçu mercredi par le ministre de la Communication René Sadi, avait déjà jugé les excuses publiques "non négociables". Pourtant, le ministre de l’Economie a fait une déclaration tendant redonner aux professionnels de la presse leur position. Une déclaration du ministre jugée insuffisante Sorti de son silence, le ministre Alamine Ousmane Mey a déclaré : « À propos des médias, j'ai une très grande estime pour la profession. J'ai du respect pour les journalistes qui en assument la responsabilité. Rien ne pourra réduire cette estime à la dimension physique d'une paire de lunettes, encore moins à sa valeur vénale. » Une phrase qui se veut apaisante, mais qui pour de nombreux observateurs et pour l'UDC, ne suffit pas. Car derrière les mots, il reste 5 jours de cellule, une humiliation publique et des journalistes sous observation médicale pendant 21 jours. Pour une paire de lunettes retrouvée dans la voiture du ministre lui-même, les professionnels attendent mieux qu'une formule : ils attendent des actes, une réparation et de vraies excuses publiques. Cet article Affaire des lunettes du ministre : L’UDC exige des excuses publiques et réparation pour les quatre journalistes humiliés est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .
data.translatedTitle: Affaire des lunettes du ministre : L’UDC exige des excuses publiques et réparation pour les quatre journalistes humiliés
data.translatedDescription: © DR L'affaire des quatre journalistes interpellés pour le vol présumé des lunettes du ministre de l’Economie, de la Planification et de l’Aménagement du Territoire Alamine Ousmane Mey prend une tournure politique. L’UDC y voit une autre forme d’atteinte à la démocratie. Dans une déclaration officielle signée de son président national, le maire Hermine Patricia Tomaino Ndam Njoya, l'Union démocratique du Cameroun (UDC) ne mâche pas ses mots. Elle exige clairement la réparation du préjudice subi par les journalistes ainsi que des excuses publiques. Pour le parti du regretté Adamou Ndam Njoya, l'incident survenu les 16 et 17 septembre 2026 en marge des Journées de la Banque islamique de développement au Palais des Congrès est "aussi insolite que fâcheux, car des plus dégradant". L'Union démocratique du Cameroun se demande comment on peut comprendre que des journalistes en plein exercice de leur métier soient confondus avec de vulgaires voleurs. Qu'ils soient à la va-vite aussi facilement jetés en cellule et à la vindicte populaire. La formation politique rappelle le fait le plus accablant : selon les déclarations des victimes, les lunettes auraient été retrouvées dès le 17 septembre à l'intérieur même du véhicule du ministre, alors que les journalistes François Essomba, Igor Gwet Bibey, Solange Djuikam et Pierre Mouchili sont restés en garde à vue au commissariat central n°1 jusqu'au 21 septembre, dans des "conditions de tristes renommées". Dénonçant un tel traitement, le parti énonce cinq exigences : il rappelle que la presse, Quatrième pouvoir, mérite considération. S’indigne de la "clochardisation de nos Médias" par le régime. Réaffirme son engagement pour une presse fière et libre. Exprime sa désolation aux quatre victimes. Et surtout, demande que réparation soit faite et que des excuses publiques soient présentées. La position de l’UDC qui rejoint celle du Syndicat national des professionnels de l’information et de la communication –SPIC- qui, reçu mercredi par le ministre de la Communication René Sadi, avait déjà jugé les excuses publiques "non négociables". Pourtant, le ministre de l’Economie a fait une déclaration tendant redonner aux professionnels de la presse leur position. Une déclaration du ministre jugée insuffisante Sorti de son silence, le ministre Alamine Ousmane Mey a déclaré : « À propos des médias, j'ai une très grande estime pour la profession. J'ai du respect pour les journalistes qui en assument la responsabilité. Rien ne pourra réduire cette estime à la dimension physique d'une paire de lunettes, encore moins à sa valeur vénale. » Une phrase qui se veut apaisante, mais qui pour de nombreux observateurs et pour l'UDC, ne suffit pas. Car derrière les mots, il reste 5 jours de cellule, une humiliation publique et des journalistes sous observation médicale pendant 21 jours. Pour une paire de lunettes retrouvée dans la voiture du ministre lui-même, les professionnels attendent mieux qu'une formule : ils attendent des actes, une réparation et de vraies excuses publiques. Cet article Affaire des lunettes du ministre : L’UDC exige des excuses publiques et réparation pour les quatre journalistes humiliés est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Cameroun : deux candidats pour succéder à Maurice Kamto, la convention du MRC se précise
data.description: © DR La commission électorale a bouclé l'examen des listes de candidatures, l'autorité administrative est déjà saisie pour la délivrance du récépissé de la tenue de la convention, les préparatifs annoncent les couleurs et les enjeux de l'événement. Deux listes concurrentielles sont en lice pour constituer le nouveau bureau du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun (MRC). La liste conduite par Tiriane Balbine Noah et celle de Pierre Emmanuel Binyam. Les deux ont été retenues à l'issue des travaux de la commission d'examen des dossiers de candidatures. La première déposée dans les délais, remplit tous les critères personnels des membres et du groupe exigés pour faire acte de candidature. Il s'agit entre autres des critères de l'âge, de la régularité de la qualité de membre du parti, du paiement de la caution de 500 000 FCFA... D'après les conclusions de la commission électorale, il n'est reproché à cette liste aucun manquement pouvant entraîner sa disqualification. Tous les dossiers de la liste « sont conformes aux dispositions... des statuts du MRC ». La deuxième liste retenue, celle conduite par Pierre Emmanuel Binyam, est aussi admise. Mais la commission précise que son admission a été décidée à la suite d'un examen approfondi et grâce à la flexibilité du de la commission. Il était reproché à cette liste certains manquements dont l'irrégularité des cotisations annuelles de six des huit membres de la liste, la proposition d'un second formulaire de la liste déposée en retard, des justificatifs de la régularité des cotisations postérieures à la date limite du dépôt des candidatures. Mais après délibérations «la commission a décidé de ne pas imposer ces irrégularités à la liste de M. Binyam Pierre Emmanuel et de l'admettre à participer à la compétition électorale prévue lors de la Convention Extraordinaire du 17 octobre 2026 ». Après la publication des conclusions de la commission, un communiqué attribué à Pierre Emmanuel Binyam fait savoir aux militants que la commission électorale n'a pas eu besoin de manifester de l'indulgence pour la validation de sa liste. « Nous avons rempli toutes les conditions d’éligibilité ». Réaction que Aissatou Bouba Dalil qualifie de « mauvaise foi de Pierre Emmanuel Binyam ». Elle insiste sur la vérité de tout ce que la commission électorale a écrit dans le procès-verbal. Tout compte fait, toutes ces réactions n'influencent en rien la suite du processus. Le 23 septembre, le secrétaire général du parti, Roger Justin Noah, président de la commission électorale, a saisi le sous-préfet de Yaoundé 4 à l'effet de déclarer la réunion pour la tenue de la convention du 17 octobre au siège du MRC au quartier Odza à Yaoundé. Le parti sollicite de l'autorité administrative la délivrance du récépissé de déclaration. Cet article Cameroun : deux candidats pour succéder à Maurice Kamto, la convention du MRC se précise est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .
